question_text:
Conservators opening a leather satchel dredged from the Dunmarrow millrace in 2016 found that tucked inside its lining ______ two bone dice and a boxwood tally stick, objects that had gone unnoticed for six centuries.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. The conventions being tested are subject-verb agreement and verb tense. In the clause that follows "found that," the phrase "tucked inside its lining" comes first, so the subject of the clause comes after the verb: "two bone dice and a boxwood tally stick." This compound subject is plural, so the verb must be plural, even though the singular noun "lining" sits right before the blank. The clause also reports what the conservators found in 2016, a completed event in the past, so the simple past tense is needed. "Were" is the plural, simple past form of the verb.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect. The simple past tense is right, but the singular verb "was" doesn't agree in number with the plural compound subject "two bone dice and a boxwood tally stick." It agrees only with the singular noun "lining," which is part of the fronted phrase "tucked inside its lining" and is not the subject.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. The plural verb "have been" agrees with the compound subject, but it is in the present perfect tense, which describes a situation continuing up to the present. The clause reports what conservators found at a completed point in the past (2016), following the past tense verb "found," so the simple past is required.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. "Being" is a non-finite participle, not a finite verb. Used here, it leaves the clause that begins with "that" without a finite verb, so "two bone dice and a boxwood tally stick" has no predicate and the clause is incomplete.

question_text:
The survey that the Vennick River Authority commissioned after the floods of 2014, which mapped every culvert, levee, and drainage channel along the Tarrow basin's three tributaries, ______ that nearly half of the structures were built before modern design standards existed.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice D is the best answer. The convention being tested is the formation of a complete main verb that agrees with its subject. The subject of the sentence is the singular noun "survey." Everything between "survey" and the blank ("that the Vennick River Authority commissioned after the floods of 2014" and "which mapped every culvert, levee, and drainage channel along the Tarrow basin's three tributaries") is a pair of modifying clauses, each with its own verb ("commissioned," "mapped"), so the sentence has not yet supplied a main verb for "survey." The singular, finite verb "reveals" completes the predicate and agrees in number with "survey," and the "that" clause that follows names what the survey revealed.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because the plural verb "reveal" doesn't agree in number with the singular subject "survey." It agrees only with the nearby plural noun "tributaries," which is part of a modifying clause and is not the subject of the sentence.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because the participle "revealing" is a nonfinite verb form, which can't serve as the main verb of a sentence. Using it leaves "The survey ... revealing that nearly half ..." without a finite predicate, so the sentence is a fragment.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because it inserts the pronoun "it" as a second subject. The sentence already has a subject, "The survey," and the pronoun "it" repeats that subject immediately before the verb. Standard English doesn't allow a redundant subject pronoun to restate a subject that has already been named in the same clause, so "The survey ..., it reveals" is ungrammatical even though "reveals" is the correct singular verb.

question_text:
Since 2004, translating the Ostvelt lute makers' surviving account books ______ that the workshop bought its spruce soundboards not from nearby forests, as historians long assumed, but from traders in distant Alpine valleys.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice B is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement combined with verb tense. The subject of the sentence is the gerund phrase "translating the Ostvelt lute makers' surviving account books," which names a single activity and therefore takes a singular verb; the plural noun "books" is only the object inside that phrase. In addition, the opening phrase "Since 2004" marks a span of time that began in the past and continues to the present, which calls for the present perfect tense. "Has revealed" is a finite, singular, present perfect verb, so it satisfies both requirements.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because it uses the simple present tense, which cannot be combined with "Since 2004." That phrase marks a period that began in the past and extends to now, and a period of that kind requires the present perfect ("has revealed"). The verb does agree in number with the singular subject, so the error is in tense only.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect because "have" is a plural verb and does not agree in number with the singular subject, the gerund phrase "translating ... books." The plural noun "books" right before the blank is not the subject, so it does not control the verb. The present perfect tense is correct here, so the error is in subject-verb agreement only.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because "having revealed" is a participle, not a finite verb, so the sentence has no main verb and is a fragment. A sentence needs a finite verb, one that carries tense and agrees with its subject, to go with the subject "translating ... books." The perfect aspect is appropriate for the "Since 2004" time frame, but the form is non-finite.

question_text:
During the drought of 2008, not one of the eleven seed varieties that the Quessel Valley cooperative's growers were testing in experimental plots ______ capable of matching the district's average yield without supplemental irrigation.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice A is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement, along with verb tense. The subject of the sentence is the singular pronoun "one" ("not one of the eleven seed varieties ..."), so the main verb must be singular. The long phrase "of the eleven seed varieties that the Quessel Valley cooperative's growers were testing in experimental plots" follows "one" (the relative clause inside it modifies "varieties") but does not change the number of "one". The introductory phrase "During the drought of 2008" sets the whole sentence in a completed period in the past, so the simple past tense is required. "Was" is the singular simple past form and is therefore the only choice that agrees with the subject and fits the time frame.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect. "Were" is in the correct tense (simple past), but it is plural and doesn't agree in number with the singular subject "one." The plural noun "varieties" and the plural verb "were testing" inside the relative clause sit between the subject and the blank, but they belong to the modifying phrase, not to the subject of the main verb.
distractor_c_explanation: Choice C is incorrect. "Has been" agrees in number with the singular subject "one," but it is in the present perfect tense, which is used for situations that continue up to the present. The introductory phrase "During the drought of 2008" sets the main clause in a specific, completed period in the past, and the present perfect can't be used with a finished past time frame like that one, so the simple past is required.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect. "Being" is a non-finite (participle) form that cannot serve as the main verb of a sentence. Using it leaves the subject "not one of the eleven seed varieties ..." without a finite verb, which results in a sentence fragment.

question_text:
The ferry schedule posted at the north pier of Halvern Cove and the fare table printed on the back of the island boarding pass ______ the closing hours of the town's shops for the past decade.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
explanation: Choice C is the best answer. The convention being tested is subject-verb agreement, together with verb tense. The subject of the sentence is a compound: "The ferry schedule ... and the fare table." Two separate things joined by "and" make a plural subject, even though each noun is singular and the singular noun "pass" sits right before the blank. A plural subject requires a plural verb, so "have" is needed. The phrase "for the past decade" describes a period that began in the past and continues to the present, which calls for the present perfect tense. "Have determined" is a plural verb in the present perfect.
distractor_a_explanation: Choice A is incorrect because "has determined" is a singular verb and doesn't agree in number with the plural compound subject "the ferry schedule ... and the fare table." It agrees only with the nearby singular noun "pass," which is part of a modifier and is not the subject.
distractor_b_explanation: Choice B is incorrect because "determine" is in the simple present tense. The phrase "for the past decade" describes a span of time that began in the past and continues up to now, so it requires the present perfect, not the simple present. The verb number is correct (plural), but the tense is not.
distractor_d_explanation: Choice D is incorrect because "having determined" is a non-finite participial form and can't serve as the main verb. Used here, it leaves the sentence without a finite verb, so the long compound subject has no predicate and the result is a sentence fragment.
